package.name: Unicode
package.description: Unicode character properties, case, normalization and segmentation

modules.name: Case
modules.header:
Case, without a locale.
Three kinds of mapping live here and they answer different questions. The simple mappings take one scalar value
to one: cheap, allocation-free, and wrong for the handful of characters whose case changes their length — a
sharp s uppercases to two letters, which one-to-one cannot say. The full mappings say it, writing up to three
values. And folding is neither case: it is the canonical form two strings are taken to before asking whether
they are the same text, chosen so the answer is the same in every locale.
What is deliberately absent is everything conditional. A dotless i is what `i` uppercases to in Turkish and not
elsewhere; a final sigma depends on where in the word it stands. Those rules exist, are in the data, and are not
here, because applying them silently is how text changes meaning by passing through a machine set to the wrong
language. A caller with a locale applies its rules knowingly, on top.

modules.name: Graphemes
modules.header:
Where one user-perceived character ends and the next begins.
A scalar value is not a character as a reader counts them: an e and its acute are two values and one thing on the
screen, a family emoji is seven values and one glyph, a Hangul syllable typed as jamo is three. The extended
grapheme cluster is Unicode's answer to "what does one arrow-key press cross", and these are the UAX #29 rules
that define it, the emoji and Indic conjunct rules included.
The interface is one question: is there a boundary before position N. Everything else — counting clusters,
walking them — is a loop over that question, and the committed break vectors hold every rule to the standard's
own test file.

modules.name: Lookup
modules.header:
Binary search over the generated tables.
Every table is a flat, sorted `uint32` array: pairs of (first, last) for a boolean property, triples of
(first, last, value) where a range carries one, and (key, offset, length) index triples over an element pool
where a code point maps to a sequence. Three searches serve all of them, and everything else in the package is
written against these rather than against the arrays' shapes.

modules.name: Normalize
modules.header:
The four normal forms, over scalar values.
Normalization is what makes "the same text" a checkable claim: an e-with-acute is one scalar value or two, and a
comparison that has not normalized calls them different. NFD takes everything apart canonically and orders the
marks; NFC puts back together what has a composed form; the K forms do the same after compatibility
decomposition, which also flattens ligatures, width variants and the like — a bigger hammer, for callers who
mean "the same characters" more loosely.
Everything works on slices of scalar values and writes into a caller's buffer, reporting the length or refusing
for want of room; nothing here allocates. Text-level normalization is a walk over a string's scalars into one of
these and back out through a builder, and belongs beside the text types rather than here.
Hangul is arithmetic throughout: a syllable decomposes into its jamo and recomposes from them by formula, which
is why none of it is in the tables.

modules.name: Properties
modules.header:
What kind of character a scalar value is.
Every answer is a binary search over the generated ranges, so a property costs a handful of comparisons and no
table costs more memory than its ranges. The category ordinals mirror `GeneralCategory` exactly; the table
stores numbers, and this enum is what the numbers mean.

items.name: Fold
items.signature: pub func Fold(scalar: char32, into: var char32[..], written: *var uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Writes the full, locale-independent case folding of `scalar` into `into`.
doc.markdown:
Writes the full, locale-independent case folding of `scalar` into `into`.
Folding is for comparison rather than display: fold both strings, and equal foldings mean the same text
whatever its case. It is built from the C and F entries alone, which is what makes the answer the same in every
locale. A point with no entry folds to itself.
`written` must be non-null and writable.

params.name: into
params.markdown: receives the folding; three values always suffice

params.markdown: receives how many values were written

items.name: IsGraphemeBoundary
items.signature: pub func IsGraphemeBoundary(text: char32[..], index: uint) -> bool

doc.summary: Whether a cluster boundary falls before `index` in `text`.
doc.markdown:
Whether a cluster boundary falls before `index` in `text`.
The ends count: position zero and the length are always boundaries, which is what makes "the clusters of a
text" a partition of it. The rules between are UAX #29's, applied to the pair either side of the position with
lookback where a rule reaches further — the emoji join, the flag pairs, and the Indic conjuncts.
Runs in time proportional to the lookback, which is the run of marks behind the position; allocates nothing.

params.name: index
params.markdown: the position to test, in scalar values

doc.returns: whether a grapheme cluster boundary falls before `index`
